verses.1: Al-Mizan identifies al-qāriʿah as a Qur’anic name for the Resurrection, from qarʿ, a severe and massive blow; the next verse supplies its predicate. It reports that exegetes call it this because it strikes hearts with fear and God’s enemies with punishment.
verses.2: Al-Mizan says the rhetorical question, despite the Pounder being known, conveys its overwhelming terror and the unfathomable reality of the Resurrection.
verses.3: Al-Mizan says the question of what could teach the Pounder further emphasizes the Day of Resurrection’s immensity.
verses.4: Al-Mizan treats ‘the day’ as a temporal qualification of an omitted verb. A report from al-Farrāʾ defines farāsh as a mob of locusts carpeting the ground and climbing over one another. People emerging from graves are compared to locusts because terror makes them fly hither and thither without direction; alternatively, they head toward their differing abodes of happiness or misery.
verses.5: Al-Mizan explains ʿihn as multicolored wool and nafsh as spreading wool with a card or similar tool. The image of carded wool signifies that, when the Hour comes and the earth quakes, mountains of all their colors will crumble.
verses.6: Al-Mizan takes the scales to weigh deeds: faith and acts of obedience are weighty and valued by God, while kufr and disobedience have neither weight nor standing. Their consequences differ accordingly, yielding happiness or misery. A pleased ʿīshah is a particular kind of life; ‘pleased’ is figurative for its inhabitant’s pleasure, or abbreviates dhāt riḍā, a life characterized by pleasure.

verses.8: Al-Mizan apparently identifies hāwiyah with hell, named for the plunging descent of one cast into its depths, and calls fire so figuratively as it called life ‘pleased.’ Umm means the person’s final abode and place of return, like a child’s recourse to a mother. It rejects the alternative umm al-raʾs, which would mean being cast into hell headfirst, because the next verse’s pronoun would then lack an antecedent.

verses.10: Al-Mizan says the verse interprets hāwiyah in the previous verse and intensifies the enormity of that fire; its pronoun refers back to hāwiyah. The final h is a pause, waqf.
verses.11: Al-Mizan identifies hāwiyah as a ḥāmiyah, scorching-hot fire.
